reference.source: Parsons' Diseases of the Eye / Kanski Clinical Ophthalmology
clinicalPearls: Typically presents with painless blurred vision and floaters rather than the pain and redness seen with anterior involvement
Inflammation centres on the choroid and retina, so signs are found on fundus examination as vitritis, focal or multifocal chorioretinal lesions, and vascular sheathing
Vitreous haze grading gives a useful measure of activity and treatment response
Toxoplasma retinochoroiditis is a leading infective cause and characteristically produces a focal lesion adjacent to an old pigmented scar
Non-infective causes include sarcoidosis, Behcet disease, sympathetic ophthalmia, and the white-dot syndromes
Distinguishing infective from immune-mediated aetiology is essential because immunosuppression can worsen an untreated infection
Management of non-infective disease relies on corticosteroids and steroid-sparing immunosuppression, whereas infective disease requires targeted antimicrobial cover first
Complications that threaten sight include cystoid macular oedema, retinal detachment, choroidal neovascular membranes, and optic nerve involvement
reference.pathophysiology: Posterior uveitis is inflammation predominantly affecting the choroid and overlying retina, often with secondary vitreous involvement. It may arise from direct infection (for example Toxoplasma, tuberculosis, syphilis, viral retinitis) or from immune-mediated processes such as sarcoidosis, Behcet disease, or an autoimmune reaction to ocular antigens as in sympathetic ophthalmia. Inflammatory cells and mediators disrupt the outer blood-retinal barrier, causing exudation, oedema, and eventual chorioretinal scarring. Ischaemia and chronic inflammation can drive neovascularisation, and macular or optic nerve involvement determines the visual outcome.
additionalDifferentials: Intraocular lymphoma masquerading as chronic vitritis
Retinal vein occlusion with macular oedema
Age-related macular degeneration with choroidal neovascular membrane
additionalInvestigations: Dilated fundus examination and vitreous haze grading to assess activity
Optical coherence tomography to detect macular oedema and monitor response
Fundus fluorescein and indocyanine green angiography to map retinal and choroidal inflammation
Serology and targeted testing for toxoplasma, syphilis, tuberculosis, and sarcoidosis
Vitreous or aqueous sampling with PCR or cytology when infection or lymphoma is suspected
Systemic imaging (e.g. chest imaging) when sarcoidosis or tuberculosis is considered
redFlags: Rapidly progressive retinitis suggesting viral (necrotising) infection needing urgent antiviral therapy
Bilateral panuveitis after ocular injury or surgery raising concern for sympathetic ophthalmia
Persistent vitritis in an older patient that may represent intraocular lymphoma
Macular or optic nerve involvement with declining acuity requiring prompt treatment
reference.prognosis: Outcome depends on the underlying cause and on whether the macula and optic nerve are spared; focal treatable infections such as toxoplasmosis often heal with scarring away from the fovea, but recurrent or immune-mediated disease can cause cumulative visual loss from macular oedema, scarring, or neovascular complications.
pitfalls: Starting immunosuppression before excluding an infective cause, which can allow infection to progress
Overlooking cystoid macular oedema as the reason for reduced acuity in a quiet-looking eye
Attributing chronic vitritis in an older patient to inflammation and missing masquerade lymphoma
Failing to screen for a systemic disease that the eye findings are heralding
